prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: Restaurant Dinner Menu (language en).
Grid: 4 columns × 9 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Merged cells: "Starters" spans 4 col × 1 row; "Mains" spans 4 col × 1 row; "Desserts" spans 4 col × 1 row.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Dish" · longest unbreakable word 77px · one-line width 164px
  col 2: header "Description" · longest unbreakable word 83px · one-line width 558px
  col 3: header "Price" · longest unbreakable word 37px · one-line width 37px
  col 4: header "Allergens" · longest unbreakable word 70px · one-line width 298px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 563px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 562px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""},"F":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

The narrow price column and generous allergen column make good use of the width."},"B":{"grade":"poor","why":"The dish column breaks “Croquettes” across lines and forces several names into three lines, while the allergen column has substantial unused space."},"C":{"grade":"poor","why":"The equal-width columns give prices excessive space and squeeze descriptions into five or six lines, making rows tall and harder to scan."},"D":{"grade":"good","why":"The wide description column reads comfortably and dish names remain intact, but the dessert allergens wrap to four lines, separating “Tree nuts” across lines."},"E":{"grade":"excellent","why":"Dish names stay within two lines, descriptions have a consistent three-line rhythm, and allergens remain readable without taking space away from the prices."},"F":{"grade":"good","why":"Descriptions and allergens fit well, but the narrower dish column pushes two dish names onto three lines, weakening their role as row identifiers."}},"best":["E"],"confidence":"high","unsure":"A is a close alternative; the preference for E rests on its slightly more balanced allocation to descriptions and allergens."}
